```{r setup, include=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8.5,
                     fig.height = 5.4, out.width = "100%", dpi = 120)
options(width = 90, digits = 4)
```

## What this case study asks

A researcher may choose categories to reveal interpretable combinations of
variables, then ask whether those categories also improve prediction. Those
are related questions, but they need not have the same answer.

This case study follows Keith A. Preble's APSA Preprints paper, *Commercial Embeddedness
and Sanctions Busting: Intra-Industry Trade, Dependence, and Economic Asymmetry*,
using fixed-effects logit models. The preprint is available at
[doi:10.33774/apsa-2026-7wxvk](https://doi.org/10.33774/apsa-2026-7wxvk).

The research concerns third-party states' trade with sanctioned targets. It
asks whether the organization of trade, dependence on the trading partner,
and differences in economic size help distinguish sanctions-busting patterns.
The example uses SITC-derived trade data.

**The lesson is not that bins are always better.** The categories organize
meaningful trade configurations and improve on a particular continuous
interaction in the prediction comparison. A flexible alternative predicts
better still. The distinction between interpretation and prediction is precisely
what a binning decision tool should make visible.

## What runs in this vignette

This guide ships small, verified **aggregate summaries of real observations**.
It recreates tables and figures from saved results; it does not reconstruct the
research panel or refit its models during package installation or checks.
There are no individual dyad-year records or fitted research models in these
bundled summaries. The full replication data are needed to rerun the regressions.

Load the package and the case-study summaries. `system.file()` locates a file
inside the installed package, so no personal folder path is needed.

```{r load-case}
library(binwise)
case <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "ii-case-study.rds", package = "binwise"))
case$metadata[c("n", "years", "events")]
```

The categorical-model sample contains **426,465 directed dyad-years from 1963
through 2023**, including 43,007 observations coded as sanctions busting. A
directed dyad-year is one third-party-to-target relationship in a given year.
These rows are not 426,465 independent countries or country pairs.

| Material | Status in this guide |
|:--|:--|
| The paper's categorical definitions, observed cells, and logit specification | Research analysis used to illustrate categorization |
| Same-sample continuous comparison and cell-mean confidence intervals | Additional diagnostic comparisons prepared for the case study |
| Grouped held-out validation and the flexible benchmark | Additional internal prediction checks prepared for binwise |

## 1. Start with what the variables mean

**Intra-industry trade, or IIT**, measures reciprocal exchange within the same
industries. Its index ranges from 0 to 1. In this setting, zero distinguishes
trade with no measured intra-industry component from positive intra-industry
exchange. It does not mean that the trading relationship itself is absent.

**Trade dependence** is the fraction of the third party's total trade accounted
for by the target. The direction matters: this is the target's importance to
the third party, not the third party's importance to the target. There are no
zero dependence values in this estimation sample.

**Economic asymmetry** is the absolute difference in the two countries' logged
GDP values. Smaller values indicate more similarly sized economies. The paper
examines whether the IIT/dependence pattern differs across economic contexts.

All three predictors used here are lagged. The sanctions-busting outcome uses
the paper's operational definition of trade expansion and target trade share.
It is an observed binary classification under that definition, not a direct
measurement of a government's intention.

## 2. Understand the category choices

The paper separates zero IIT, then divides positive IIT at its median. Dependence
uses the 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles, giving progressively finer upper-tail
groups. Economic asymmetry uses the lower quarter, middle half, and upper quarter.
These three GDP groups are sometimes called quartile-tail groups; they are not
four equal-sized quartiles.

```{r category-table}
case$bins[, c("variable", "category", "lower", "upper", "n")]
```

`lower` and `upper` are boundaries on the original numeric scales. `n` is the
number of observations assigned to a category. Values at an interior cutpoint
go into the lower interval, because these intervals include their upper endpoint.
The zero-IIT group is assigned separately.

There are 180,645 zero-IIT observations, about 42.4% of the sample. The positive
median is approximately 0.01744. The labels "lower" and "higher" positive IIT
refer to this sample's positive distribution. "Higher" does not mean near the
theoretical maximum of 1. Small count differences between positive groups arise
because equal values stay together.

**What is substantive, and what is empirical?** The zero-versus-positive
IIT distinction has substantive meaning in this application. The median and
percentile thresholds are empirical choices used to organize variation. They
are not established economic discontinuities. Their sensitivity still matters.

Look at dependence as percentages rather than fractions.

```{r dependence-percentages}
trade <- case$bins[case$bins$variable == "trade", ]
data.frame(
  category = trade$category,
  lower_percent = signif(100 * trade$lower, 4),
  upper_percent = signif(100 * trade$upper, 4),
  observations = trade$n
)
```

The boundaries are approximately **0.0524%, 0.400%, and 2.048%**. The top group
extends to about **86.2%**. These cutpoints come from the lagged estimation
sample; they should not be substituted for cutpoints computed on a different
trade dataset.

Compare that top group with ordinary quartiles.

```{r compare-ranges}
comparison <- case$trade_comparison
comparison$lower_percent <- signif(100 * comparison$lower, 4)
comparison$upper_percent <- signif(100 * comparison$upper, 4)
comparison[, c("scheme", "bin", "lower_percent", "upper_percent", "n")]
```

Ordinary quartiles put roughly 0.400% through 86.2% together. The paper divides
that interval at about 2.048%. This preserves an additional upper-tail distinction,
but its highest group remains broad. Finer categorization solves only part of
the information-loss problem.

## 3. Use heatmaps to understand the combinations

**The main finding to look for is that dependence has different patterns in
different economic contexts.** Among similarly sized economies with higher
positive IIT, sanctions busting is concentrated in the highest-dependence group.
Among highly asymmetric economies with higher positive IIT, it is concentrated
in the lower-dependence groups. The bins make these combinations easy to compare.

All three heatmaps below use the **same categories**. The first shows what
happened in the data. The second shows predictions from the paper's categorical
model at representative settings. The third subtracts the second from the first.
The comparison with continuous models comes later in the guide.

### First, learn what one square means

Each square, or **cell**, collects observations with one combination of three
characteristics. Use these directions to find a cell in the first heatmap.

| Part of the figure | What it identifies |
|:--|:--|
| Panel | How similar the two economies are in size. The left panel contains the most similar economies; the right panel contains the most asymmetric. |
| Row | The IIT group. The bottom row is zero IIT, the middle row is the lower half of positive IIT, and the top row is the upper half of positive IIT. |
| Column | The dependence group, increasing from left to right. For example, `90-100` means the highest tenth of the dependence distribution, not dependence between 90% and 100%. |
| Percentage inside the square | The fraction of observations in that cell classified as sanctions busting. |
| `n` inside the square | The number of dyad-year observations in the cell, including both busting and non-busting observations. |

Find the **top-right square of the Similar economies panel**. It combines
similarly sized economies, higher positive IIT, and the highest dependence
group. Its label is **70.7%, n = 4,909**. That means 3,469 of those 4,909
dyad-years were classified as sanctions busting. It does not mean that the
cell contains 70.7% of all sanctions-busting observations in the dataset.

There are 36 cells in total. The panels use the GDP groups introduced in
Section 2, consisting of the lower quarter, middle half, and upper quarter of
economic asymmetry. Every panel shares the same color scale. Darker squares
have higher rates, not necessarily more observations.

```{r heatmap-helper, echo=FALSE}
gdp_groups <- case$metadata$levels$gdp
trade_groups <- case$metadata$levels$trade
paper_cells <- case$paper_heatmaps[case$paper_heatmaps$strategy == "quartile", ]
draw_paper_heatmap <- function(measure, title, difference = FALSE) {
  old <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old))
  layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE), heights = c(5, 1.5))
  par(oma = c(2, 0, 2, 0))
  limits <- if (difference) c(-100, 100) else c(0, 100)
  palette <- if (difference) {
    colorRampPalette(c("#2166AC", "#F7F7F7", "#B2182B"))(201)
  } else colorRampPalette(c("#F7FCF0", "#74A9CF", "#034E7B"))(201)
  titles <- c("Similar economies", "Moderately different", "Highly asymmetric")
  for (j in seq_along(gdp_groups)) {
    par(mar = c(3, 4.5, 2, .5))
    z <- paper_cells[paper_cells$gdp_similarity_bin == gdp_groups[j], ]
    at_x <- match(z$tpts_bin, trade_groups)
    at_y <- match(z$iit_model_bin, case$metadata$levels$iit)
    value <- 100 * z[[measure]]
    index <- 1L + round(200 * (value - limits[1]) / diff(limits))
    fill <- palette[pmax(1L, pmin(201L, index))]
    luminance <- colSums(col2rgb(fill) * c(.2126, .7152, .0722)) / 255
    ink <- ifelse(luminance < .5, "white", "#18252B")
    plot.new()
    plot.window(xlim = c(.5, 4.5), ylim = c(.5, 3.5), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
    rect(at_x - .5, at_y - .5, at_x + .5, at_y + .5, col = fill, border = "white")
    labels <- if (difference) ifelse(abs(value) < .05, "0.0", sprintf("%+.1f", value)) else
      sprintf("%.1f%%", value)
    text(at_x, at_y + .12, labels, col = ink, cex = 1)
    text(at_x, at_y - .16, paste0("n=", format(z$n, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)),
         col = ink, cex = .8)
    axis(1, 1:4, c("0-50", "50-75", "75-90", "90-100"), tick = FALSE, cex.axis = .8)
    axis(2, 1:3, c("Zero IIT", "Lower\npositive IIT", "Higher\npositive IIT"),
         tick = FALSE, las = 1, cex.axis = .75)
    title(main = titles[j], cex.main = .95)
  }
  par(mar = c(3.5, 7, .5, 7))
  plot.new()
  plot.window(xlim = limits, ylim = c(0, 1), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  edges <- seq(limits[1], limits[2], length.out = length(palette) + 1L)
  rect(head(edges, -1), 0, tail(edges, -1), 1, col = palette, border = NA)
  axis(1, at = if (difference) seq(-100, 100, 50) else seq(0, 100, 25), cex.axis = .8)
  mtext(if (difference) "Observed minus representative probability (percentage points)" else
    "Sanctions-busting rate or probability (%)", 1, line = 2.3, cex = .8)
  mtext(title, 3, outer = TRUE, line = .5)
  mtext("Columns show trade-dependence percentile groups; each tile has equal display area",
        1, outer = TRUE, line = 0, cex = .7)
}
```

```{r observed-heatmap, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.3}
draw_paper_heatmap("observed_rate", "Observed sanctions-busting rates")
```

### Now make three comparisons

**1. Move across the top row of Similar economies.** The observed rates are
0.1%, 3.5%, 28.8%, and 70.7%. Within this economic-size and IIT combination,
higher dependence groups have higher sanctions-busting rates. The largest
rate is in the top-right square you just identified.

**2. Move to the same top row in Highly asymmetric economies.** The rates are
34.7%, 41.9%, 7.3%, and 2.3%. Here, the two lower-dependence groups have much
higher rates than the two upper-dependence groups. The highest-dependence
square has a rate of only 2.3%, compared with 70.7% in the corresponding square
for similar economies. The middle panel shows another pattern, rising from
3.5% to 33.9% across that row, with much less change between its last two groups.

**3. Look down the first column of Highly asymmetric economies.** The rate
is 34.7% for higher positive IIT, 32.4% for lower positive IIT, and 5.2% for
zero IIT. In this low-dependence group, the distinction between zero and
positive IIT is especially visible. Looking only at dependence would miss it.

### What does binning contribute here?

The substantive conclusion is that **dependence, IIT, and economic asymmetry
need to be interpreted together**. A statement such as "higher dependence is
associated with more sanctions busting" describes some combinations poorly.
The heatmap lets a reader identify which combinations have high or low rates
without having to interpret a set of interaction coefficients.

This is a reason to consider categories for **description and communication**.
The bins turn three numeric variables into a manageable set of comparisons.
They summarize a pattern already present in the observations; they do not
create it. Flexible continuous models can also represent such patterns. Later
sections ask whether using categories in the prediction model improves accuracy.

Binning also hides variation. Each square contains observations with different
numeric values, and equal-sized squares can contain very different numbers of
observations. In the similar-economy, zero-IIT row, for example, the rightmost
cell has only 194 observations, while the leftmost has 41,276. Read the counts
alongside the percentages. Uncertainty intervals are needed to assess precision.
These descriptive patterns alone establish neither a causal effect nor a
special economic threshold at an exact cutpoint.

### Next, distinguish observed rates from model predictions

The second heatmap asks what probability the **categorical model** assigns to
each combination at representative settings for the other variables. Those
other variables include the model's controls and fixed effects. The prediction
uses selected settings, such as group-specific means or medians for controls
and a common year, rather than the actual covariates of every observation in
the cell.

Think of each square as a constructed example of that combination. Its
prediction answers, "What probability does the model give this combination
at these settings?" The first heatmap instead answers, "What fraction of the
observations in this combination actually experienced sanctions busting?"
These are different summaries, so they need not be equal.

Both heatmaps below and above use the same categories and 0-100% scale.
Percentages are rounded to one decimal place; a displayed 0.0% can represent
a small positive probability.

```{r representative-heatmap, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.3}
draw_paper_heatmap("representative_probability", "Representative model-implied probabilities")
```

Return to the **top-right square in Similar economies**. The first heatmap
reports an observed rate of 70.7%; this one gives a representative prediction
of 57.4%. The categorical model still assigns this combination a relatively
high probability, but the prediction for the chosen settings is below the
observed cell rate.

Now inspect the **top row, second column in Highly asymmetric economies**.
The observed rate is 41.9%, whereas the representative prediction is about
0.3%. The difference is much larger. This is a reason to examine how the
chosen representative settings compare with the observations in that cell.
It is not yet a measure of how well the model predicts those actual observations.

### Finally, use the difference heatmap to locate the gaps

Each value in the third heatmap is calculated as

**observed cell rate minus representative predicted probability**.

Red squares have positive differences, meaning the observed rate is higher.
Blue squares have negative differences, meaning the representative prediction
is higher. White is close to zero. Unlike the first two maps, this map measures
**percentage-point differences**.

```{r difference-heatmap, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.3}
draw_paper_heatmap("observed_minus_representative",
                   "Observed minus representative model predictions", difference = TRUE)
```

Follow these three examples through the maps. All use higher positive IIT,
the top row.

| Economic-size panel and dependence group | Observed rate | Representative prediction | Difference |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Similar economies, 90-100 | 70.7% | 57.4% | +13.3 percentage points |
| Highly asymmetric economies, 50-75 | 41.9% | 0.3% | +41.6 percentage points |
| Highly asymmetric economies, 90-100 | 2.3% | 21.3% | -19.0 percentage points |

For the first row, subtracting 57.4 from 70.7 gives +13.3. The red square
means the observed rate is higher. For the last row, subtracting 21.3 from
2.3 gives -19.0. The blue square means the representative prediction is higher.

These gaps help locate combinations worth examining. Their size can reflect
both the model specification and how representative settings differ from the
actual mix of observations. They are not held-out prediction errors or tests
of statistical significance. In particular, they do not show that bins perform
better or worse than continuous predictors, because all three maps use the
same categories and only the categorical model appears in the prediction map.

**The takeaway from the heatmaps is an interpretable pattern of joint
combinations.** The next step is to assess the model using predictions for
the actual observations, followed by uncertainty intervals and held-out tests.
That separates the usefulness of bins for explaining a pattern from their
usefulness for predicting new observations.

## 4. Separate descriptive agreement from model evidence

The paper's categorical specification includes all joint IIT/dependence/GDP
cell effects, controls, year fixed effects, and sanction-configuration fixed
effects. Standard errors are clustered by third-party and target country.

An additional benchmark retains continuous IIT and dependence, their interaction,
and interactions with the GDP groups. The remaining controls and fixed effects
are held consistent. Averaging each model's predictions over the **same observed
rows in each cell** gives a comparable diagnostic.

```{r fitted-cell-agreement}
max(abs(case$observed_cells$observed - case$observed_cells$categorical))
```

The difference is extremely small. With this unpenalized logit specification,
the joint cell effects make the fitted cell averages reproduce observed cell
rates, up to numerical tolerance. That in-sample agreement is expected from
the model's score equations. It is not independent evidence that the cutpoints
are right, or that the categories will predict new observations well.

The representative-prediction heatmap above uses a different quantity from
predictions averaged over observed rows. There is no contradiction between its
nonzero differences and the near-exact cell-average agreement here. The next
figure is the added **cell-average diagnostic**, with confidence intervals.

## 5. Add uncertainty without overstating what it resolves

These intervals describe fitted mean probabilities, conditional on the
selected bins and observed covariates. They incorporate year and configuration
coefficients using explicit indicators and two-way country-clustered covariance.
They are not intervals for individual binary outcomes.

```{r fitted-cell-intervals}
ci <- case$confidence[
  case$confidence$iit_model_bin == "Positive IIT: 50-100th pct.", ]
local({
  old <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old))
  par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1), oma = c(2, 0, 2, 0))
  for (j in seq_along(gdp_groups)) {
    z <- ci[ci$gdp_similarity_bin == gdp_groups[j], ]
    plot(NA_real_, NA_real_, xlim = c(.8, 4.2), ylim = c(0, 100), xaxt = "n",
         xlab = "", ylab = "Cell mean probability (%)",
         main = c("Similar economies", "Moderately different", "Highly asymmetric")[j])
    axis(1, 1:4, c("0-50", "50-75", "75-90", "90-100"), las = 2)
    for (m in c("continuous", "categorical")) {
      a <- z[z$model == m, ]
      a <- a[match(trade_groups, a$tpts_bin), ]
      at <- 1:4 + if (m == "continuous") -.06 else .06
      color <- if (m == "continuous") "#397985" else "#CC6848"
      lines(at, 100 * a$estimate, type = "b", pch = 16, col = color)
      arrows(at, 100 * a$lower, at, 100 * a$upper,
             angle = 90, code = 3, length = .03, col = color)
      if (m == "categorical") points(1:4, 100 * a$observed, pch = 1)
    }
    if (j == 1) legend("topleft", c("Observed", "Continuous", "Categorical"),
      col = c("black", "#397985", "#CC6848"), pch = c(1, 16, 16), bty = "n", cex = .75)
  }
  mtext("Higher positive IIT, with 95% pointwise intervals", 3, outer = TRUE, line = .5)
  mtext("Trade-dependence percentile group; model-based cell means with clustered covariance",
        1, outer = TRUE, line = .3, cex = .75)
})
```

The continuous benchmark smooths over parts of the observed pattern. The
intervals describe uncertainty under the fitted specifications; their overlap
is not a paired test of differences between models.

The covariance estimator required a positive-semidefinite adjustment in both
explicit-indicator fits. This warning is retained in `case$confidence_checks`.
These intervals depend on the fitted model and covariance assumptions. Neither
these intervals nor the later score intervals account for uncertainty from
choosing the categories.

## 6. Ask a different question with held-out predictions

The additional validation holds out **unordered country pairs** in five folds.
Both directions and all years of a pair stay together. The models predict rows
for a pair they did not fit. This assesses generalization across pairs during
the observed period. It does not assess forecasting later years or entirely
new countries.

Within each training fold, the workflow learns the positive-IIT median, trade
percentiles, GDP cutpoints, and spline knots. The outcome definition, including
its previously calculated sanctions-busting threshold, remains fixed. This
validation does not repeat the upstream construction of the outcome labels.

| Candidate | Representation |
|:--|:--|
| `continuous` | Linear IIT and dependence terms, their product, and interactions with GDP groups |
| `categorical` | Joint IIT/dependence/GDP categories following the paper's grouping rule |
| `flexible` | Natural splines for IIT and log-transformed dependence, a positive-IIT indicator, and the original IIT-by-dependence product, interacted with GDP groups |

The flexible specification uses three-degree-of-freedom splines. Dependence is
transformed as `log1p(100 * share)`, meaning the logarithm of one plus its value
in percentage points. The positive-IIT indicator preserves the meaningful
zero distinction. All candidates retain the same outcome, controls, and fixed
effects. All 15 final fold fits converged, and all 426,465 observations received
predictions from all three candidates.

**This is not the same model as setting `spline_df = 3` in `bin_interact()`.**
The paper needs three-way structure, fixed effects, and its specific zero and
transformation terms. Its validation used `bin_validate()` with an advanced
`fit_predict` callback and the research estimator. The generic built-in spline
option is a simpler model interface.

```{r heldout-scores}
case$scores[, c("model", "metric", "score", "lower", "upper")]
```

The **Brier score** is the average squared difference between predicted
probability and the observed 0/1 outcome. **Log loss** penalizes confident wrong
predictions particularly strongly. Lower is better for both. These are losses,
not percentages of correct classifications. A Brier score of 0.042 does not
mean that 4.2% of observations were classified incorrectly.

The categories improve on the continuous benchmark, while the flexible model
has the lowest pooled loss. That ordering also holds within each fold.

```{r fold-results}
case$fold_scores[case$fold_scores$metric == "Brier", c("fold", "model", "n", "score")]
```

## 7. Compare errors on the same held-out observations

The paired comparisons subtract one model's loss from another's using the same
observations. Negative values favor the model named in `model` over `reference`.

```{r paired-differences}
case$differences
case$flexible_vs_categories
```

The categorical-minus-continuous Brier difference is about -0.00595. The
flexible-minus-categorical difference is about -0.00576. Both associated
intervals are below zero under this evaluation procedure. The log-loss
comparisons tell the same story.

The 95% intervals use 999 paired bootstrap draws resampling third-party and
target countries. Predictions and folds stay fixed. This approximates
uncertainty in the evaluation sample, not the full uncertainty from refitting,
choosing cutpoints, or selecting the preferred model. These are **internal**
checks on data previously used to develop the paper, not a newly collected,
untouched external test set.

The flexible model produced knot-adjustment messages because IIT has many
exact zeros. Covariance warnings and convergence checks are available in
`case$diagnostics` and `case$fit_checks`. These diagnostics help readers assess
fitting limitations alongside the prediction scores.

## 8. What a reader should conclude

| Question | What this example supports |
|:--|:--|
| Do the categories help communicate the substantive pattern? | They organize joint configurations and make contrasts across economic contexts visible. |
| Are all the cutpoints known economic thresholds? | No. Zero IIT has a distinct interpretation; the percentile boundaries remain empirical choices. |
| Do the categories outperform this simple continuous interaction? | Yes, in this internal prediction comparison. |
| Do they outperform the flexible alternative examined here? | No. The flexible model has lower Brier score and log loss. |
| Does prediction decide whether categories are useful for presentation? | No. Presentation and prediction can justify different representations of the same numeric variables. |
| Does this prove a causal effect or the best possible specification? | No. Those claims require additional assumptions and evidence. |

A reader could retain continuous variables with flexible terms for prediction,
while using well-described categories to communicate results. Another reader
may have a substantive reason to use a particular categorical specification.
The useful contribution of `binwise` is to make those choices and their
consequences inspectable, rather than to announce a universally best set of bins.

## 9. Recreate the categories when you have the full replication data

The following is **optional and not run in this vignette**. It requires the
426,465-row complete-case research dataset, which is not included in the
package. The aggregate `case` object above cannot substitute for individual
records when fitting the research models.

After loading that dataset into `paper_data`, these are the category-construction
steps. The original numeric columns are retained by `bin_apply()`.

```{r full-data-categories, eval=FALSE}
iit_scheme <- bin_diagnose(paper_data, "iit_lag", bins = 2,
                           separate_zero = TRUE, warn = FALSE)
trade_scheme <- bin_diagnose(
  paper_data, "thirdparty_trade_share_lag", method = "custom",
  breaks = as.numeric(quantile(paper_data$thirdparty_trade_share_lag,
                              c(0, .5, .75, .9, 1))), warn = FALSE
)
gdp_scheme <- bin_diagnose(
  paper_data, "gdp_similarity_lag1", method = "custom",
  breaks = as.numeric(quantile(paper_data$gdp_similarity_lag1,
                              c(0, .25, .75, 1))), warn = FALSE
)
paper_binned <- bin_apply(paper_data, iit_scheme, name = "iit_binned")
paper_binned <- bin_apply(paper_binned, trade_scheme, name = "trade_binned")
paper_binned <- bin_apply(paper_binned, gdp_scheme, name = "gdp_binned")
```

These steps reproduce the paper's three category definitions while retaining
the original numeric variables. Full-sample definitions describe the observed
data; for predictive validation, learn definitions within each training fold
instead. The paper's fixed-effects models also require its controls and
estimation specification.

## Provenance and citation

The summary bundle is documented in `?ii_case_study`. Source-file hashes and
relative paths are available in `case$provenance`. The figures and tables use
precomputed research results. Running this vignette reproduces their presentation,
not the underlying regressions. The additional model comparisons and internal
validation illustrate the binwise workflow.

Preble, Keith (2026). *Commercial Embeddedness and Sanctions Busting:
Intra-Industry Trade, Dependence, and Economic Asymmetry*. APSA Preprints.
Posted November 16, 2026.
[https://doi.org/10.33774/apsa-2026-7wxvk](https://doi.org/10.33774/apsa-2026-7wxvk).
